data.targetWord: Adam — Muslims believe Adam was the first prophet and the first human, created by Allah. He was sent to earth after disobeying God in paradise, and Muslims view him as the beginning of the prophetic tradition that culminates with Muhammad.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.1 (1 mark) — Answer: A Adam

data.sourceWord: Ibrahim — friend of Allah and prophet of monotheism
data.targetWord: Muslims believe Ibrahim (Abraham) was sent by God to establish monotheistic belief and is known as Khalilullah — the friend of Allah. He broke the idols to prove the falsehood of polytheism and rebuilt the Ka'aba with his son Ismail, making him the father of the prophets.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 (2 marks) — Give two Muslim beliefs about the Prophet Ibrahim

data.sourceWord: Ibrahim — tested by God and obedient role model
data.targetWord: Muslims believe Ibrahim was severely tested by God, most notably being commanded to sacrifice his son. His willingness to obey — and his willingness to leave his wife and son in the desert — makes him a supreme role model of faith, obedience and trust in Allah.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 (2 marks) — Give two Muslim beliefs about the Prophet Ibrahim

data.targetWord: Sunni Muslims believe Allah has determined everything that will happen, recorded on the Tablet of Decrees. This influences Muslims to find comfort during hardship and grief, trusting that all good and bad comes from Allah. 'Only what God has decreed will happen to us.' (9:51)

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.3 (4 marks) — Explain two ways belief in predestination influences Muslims today

data.targetWord: Muslims also believe they have free will and will be judged on their choices. Belief in predestination influences them to perform good actions because deeds are creditworthy and recorded. Some Shi'a Muslims emphasise free will: 'God does not change the condition of a people unless they change what is in themselves.' (13:11)

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.3 (4 marks) — Explain two ways belief in predestination influences Muslims today

data.targetWord: Justice (Adl) is one of the 99 names and core qualities of Allah, especially central to Shi'a Islam as one of the Five Roots. Muslims believe God will bring everyone to account on the Day of Judgement, so fairness will ultimately prevail. This gives patience during earthly injustice.

examples.en-GB: 'Surely Allah wrongs not even of the weight of an atom.' (4:40) — AQA Q1.4 (5 marks)

data.sourceWord: God's justice — human obligation to act justly
data.targetWord: Because God is perfectly just, Muslims are called to mirror this quality on earth through giving to charity, volunteering, helping the poor, and standing up for just causes. Acting justly on earth enables Muslims to hope for God's justice in the hereafter.

examples.en-GB: 'Allah enjoins justice and fair dealing.' (16:90) — 'If you would like God to be just to you on the Day of Judgement then be just to the people.' (Hadith)

data.targetWord: 'O you who believe, be upright for God, and be bearers of witness with justice.' (5:8) — This verse commands Muslims to stand firmly for justice as a witness to God, linking divine justice with human moral duty.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.4 (5 marks) — scripture reference for God's justice

data.sourceWord: FOR: Qur'an as direct word of Allah
data.targetWord: The Qur'an is believed to be the direct, unaltered word of Allah revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril. Unlike Hadith, which can be subject to change, Allah has vowed to protect the Qur'an: 'Verily we have revealed it and we are the protectors of it.' (15:9) — making it uniquely authoritative.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.5 (12 marks) — Evaluate: 'The Qur'an is the most important authority for a Muslim'

data.sourceWord: FOR: Qur'an as comprehensive guide for life
data.targetWord: The Qur'an covers all aspects of human life and is the main source of Shari'ah Law. Those who do not judge by it are considered non-believers: 'Those who do not judge matters according to what Allah has revealed are unbelievers.' (5:44). As a complete code of life, it surpasses other sources of guidance.

examples.en-GB: 'We have sent the Scripture down to you explaining everything, and as guidance and mercy.' (16:89)

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Hadith needed for ritual practice
data.targetWord: The Qur'an does not include details of how to perform certain acts of worship such as Salah and Zakah. The Hadith (sayings and actions of the Prophet) is essential to show how these rituals are actually carried out — without it, Muslims could not practise their faith correctly, suggesting the Hadith is equally vital.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.5 (12 marks) — Arguments against 'Qur'an is the most important authority'

data.sourceWord: AGAINST: Modern life requires more than Qur'an
data.targetWord: The Qur'an was revealed over 1400 years ago and does not directly address modern technologies and ethical dilemmas such as IVF, genetic engineering, and the internet. For Shi'a Muslims, the Imam also holds great authority — equal to or greater than other sources for interpreting divine guidance in contemporary situations.
